title: 6. Schizophrenia, as was foretold
paragraphs: It was half past one in the morning when a man with a pointed beard, clad in a white coat, came out into the reception room of the famous psychiatric clinic recently built outside Moscow on the bank of the river. Three orderlies did not take their eyes off Ivan Nikolayevich, who was sitting on a couch. The extremely agitated poet Ryukhin was there too. The towels with which Ivan Nikolayevich had been tied up lay in a heap on that same couch. Ivan Nikolayevich’s hands and feet were free.
Seeing the man come in, Ryukhin turned pale, coughed and said timidly:
“Hello, doctor.”

The doctor bowed to Ryukhin, but as he bowed he looked not at him but at Ivan Nikolayevich. Ivan was sitting perfectly still, with an angry face and knitted brows, and did not even stir when the doctor came in.

“Here, doctor,” Ryukhin began, for some reason in a mysterious whisper, glancing fearfully at Ivan Nikolayevich, “the well-known poet Ivan Bezdomny... well, you see... we’re afraid it may be delirium tremens...”
“Was he drinking heavily?” the doctor asked through his teeth.
“No, he drank a bit, but not so as to...”
“Was he catching cockroaches, rats, little devils or scurrying dogs?”
“No,” Ryukhin answered with a start, “I saw him yesterday and this morning. He was perfectly healthy...”
“And why is he in long johns? Was he taken from his bed?”
“He came to the restaurant like that, doctor...”
“Aha, aha,” the doctor said, very satisfied, “and why the scratches? Was he fighting with someone?”
“He fell off a fence, and then in the restaurant he hit somebody... and somebody else as well...”
“So, so, so,” said the doctor, and, turning to Ivan, added: “Hello!”
“Hi there, wrecker!” Ivan answered loudly and spitefully.

Ryukhin was so embarrassed that he did not dare raise his eyes to the courteous doctor. But the doctor was not offended in the least; with a practiced, deft gesture he took off his glasses, lifted the skirt of his coat, put them away in the back pocket of his trousers, and then asked Ivan:
“How old are you?”
“Go to the devil, all of you, really!” Ivan shouted rudely, and turned away.
“But why are you angry? Did I say anything unpleasant to you?”
“I’m twenty-three,” Ivan began excitedly, “and I’m going to lodge a complaint against all of you. And against you in particular, you louse!” This he addressed to Ryukhin separately.
“And what is it you want to complain about?”
“About the fact that I, a healthy man, was seized and dragged by force into a madhouse!” Ivan answered in a rage.

Here Ryukhin took a close look at Ivan and went cold: there was absolutely no madness in his eyes. From being clouded, as they had been at Griboyedov’s, they had turned clear again, as they used to be.
“Good heavens!” Ryukhin thought in fright. “Is he really normal? What nonsense! Why on earth did we drag him here, then? Normal, normal, only his mug’s scratched...”
“You are,” the doctor began calmly, sitting down on a white stool with a shiny leg, “not in a madhouse but in a clinic, where nobody is going to keep you if there is no need for it.”
Ivan Nikolayevich gave him a sidelong, distrustful look, but still grumbled:
“Thank the Lord! At last there’s one normal man among the idiots, and the first of them is that dolt and no-talent Sashka!”
“Who is this no-talent Sashka?” the doctor inquired.
“Him there, Ryukhin!” Ivan answered, and jabbed a dirty finger in Ryukhin’s direction.
Ryukhin flushed with indignation.
“That’s what he gives me instead of a thank-you!” he thought bitterly. “For taking an interest in him! What a rotten creature, really!”

“A typical little kulak by his psychology,” Ivan Nikolayevich began, evidently itching to expose Ryukhin, “and, what’s more, a little kulak carefully disguising himself as a proletarian. Look at his sanctimonious face and compare it with the resounding verses he composed for the holiday on the first! Heh-heh-heh... ‘Soar on high!’ and ‘Unfurl and fly!’... but just take a look inside him—what he thinks in there... you’ll gasp!” And Ivan Nikolayevich laughed ominously.

Ryukhin was breathing heavily, red in the face, and thinking of only one thing: that he had nursed a viper in his bosom, that he had taken an interest in someone who had turned out on inspection to be a vicious enemy. And the main thing was that nothing could be done about it: one could hardly start a quarrel with a mental patient!
“And why, exactly, have you been brought to us?” the doctor asked, having listened attentively to Bezdomny’s denunciations.
“The devil take them, the blockheads! They grabbed me, tied me up with some rags and dragged me off in a truck!”
“May I ask you why you came to the restaurant in nothing but your underwear?”

“There’s nothing surprising in that,” Ivan answered. “I went for a swim in the Moscow River, and they swiped my clothes and left this rubbish! I could hardly go across Moscow naked! I put on what there was, because I was in a hurry to get to the restaurant, to Griboyedov’s.”
The doctor glanced questioningly at Ryukhin, who muttered sullenly:
“That’s the name of the restaurant.”
“Aha,” said the doctor, “and why were you in such a hurry? Some business appointment?”
“I’m trying to catch the consultant,” Ivan Nikolayevich answered, and looked round anxiously.
“What consultant?”
“Do you know Berlioz?” Ivan asked meaningfully.
“That’s... the composer?”
Ivan was upset.
“What composer? Ah, yes... No, no! The composer just has the same name as Misha Berlioz.”
Ryukhin had no wish to say anything, but he had to explain:
“Berlioz, the secretary of Massolit, was run over by a tram this evening at Patriarch’s.”
“Don’t you lie about things you know nothing about!” Ivan said angrily to Ryukhin. “It was me, not you, who was there! He set him up under the tram on purpose!”
“Pushed him?”

“What has ‘pushed’ got to do with it?” Ivan exclaimed, angered by the general obtuseness. “Someone like him doesn’t need to push! He can pull off tricks that make you hold on to your hat! He knew in advance that Berlioz would fall under a tram!”
“And did anyone besides you see this consultant?”
“That’s just the trouble, only Berlioz and I did.”

“I see. And what measures did you take to catch this murderer?” Here the doctor turned and cast a glance at a woman in a white coat sitting at a table off to one side. She took out a sheet of paper and began filling in the blanks in its columns.
“The measures were these. I took a little candle from the kitchen...”
“This one?” the doctor asked, pointing to a broken candle lying on the table next to the icon in front of the woman.
“That very one, and...”
“And why the icon?”

“Well, yes, the icon...” Ivan turned red. “It was the icon that frightened them most of all,” he again jabbed his finger toward Ryukhin, “but the thing is that he, the consultant, he... let’s speak plainly... has dealings with the unclean powers... and you won’t catch him that easily.”
The orderlies for some reason stood with their arms straight at their sides and did not take their eyes off Ivan.

“Yes,” Ivan went on, “he has dealings with them! That’s an irrefutable fact. He talked with Pontius Pilate in person. And there’s no need to look at me like that! I’m telling the truth! He saw everything—the balcony and the palms. In a word, he was with Pontius Pilate, I’ll vouch for that.”
“Go on, go on...”
“Well, so I pinned the icon on my chest and ran...”
Here the clock suddenly struck twice.
“Oho!” exclaimed Ivan, getting up from the couch. “Two o’clock, and I’m wasting time with you! Beg pardon, where’s the telephone?”
“Let him get to the telephone,” the doctor ordered the orderlies.
Ivan seized the receiver, and meanwhile the woman quietly asked Ryukhin:
“Is he married?”
“Single,” Ryukhin answered fearfully.
“Member of a trade union?”
“Yes.”

“Police?” Ivan shouted into the receiver. “Police? Comrade officer on duty, give orders at once for five motorcycles with machine guns to be sent out to capture a foreign consultant. What? Come and pick me up, I’ll go with you myself... This is the poet Bezdomny speaking, from the madhouse... What’s your address?” Bezdomny asked the doctor in a whisper, covering the receiver with his palm, and then shouted into the receiver again: “Are you listening? Hello!.. Outrageous!” Ivan suddenly howled, and flung the receiver at the wall. Then he turned to the doctor, held out his hand to him, said “goodbye” curtly, and made to leave.
“For pity’s sake, where do you mean to go?” the doctor began, peering into Ivan’s eyes. “In the dead of night, in your underwear... You are not feeling well, stay with us!”
“Let me through,” Ivan said to the orderlies, who had closed ranks at the door. “Are you going to let me through or not?” the poet shouted in a terrible voice.
Ryukhin began to tremble, and the woman pressed a button in the table, and out onto its glass surface popped a shiny little box and a sealed ampoule.
“Oh, so that’s it?!” said Ivan, looking around wildly, like a hunted animal. “All right, then! Farewell!!” And he hurled himself headfirst at the window blind.
There was a rather loud crash, but the glass behind the blind did not crack, and an instant later Ivan Nikolayevich was thrashing in the hands of the orderlies. He wheezed, tried to bite, shouted:
“So that’s the kind of glass you’ve got in here!.. Let go! Let go!..”

A syringe flashed in the doctor’s hands; with a single stroke the woman slit open the decrepit sleeve of the tolstovka and seized the arm with unwomanly strength. There was a smell of ether, Ivan went limp in the hands of four people, and the deft doctor took advantage of this moment and stuck the needle into Ivan’s arm. They held Ivan for a few more seconds and then lowered him onto the couch.

“Bandits!” Ivan shouted, and jumped up from the couch, but was put back on it again. As soon as they let go of him he started to jump up again, but this time sat back down by himself. He was silent for a while, looking around somewhat wildly, then unexpectedly yawned, then smiled spitefully.

“So you’ve locked me up after all,” he said, yawned once more, unexpectedly lay down, put his head on the pillow, his fist under his cheek like a child, and began to mutter in an already sleepy voice, without spite: “Well, so much the better... you’ll pay for it all yourselves. I’ve warned you, and now do as you like!.. What interests me most of all right now is Pontius Pilate... Pilate...” Here he closed his eyes.

“A bath, private room one hundred and seventeen, and a nurse on watch,” the doctor ordered, putting on his glasses. Here Ryukhin gave a start again: the white doors opened noiselessly, and beyond them a corridor could be seen, lit by blue night-lights. Out of the corridor rolled a couch on rubber wheels, the quieted Ivan was moved onto it, and he rolled away into the corridor, and the doors closed behind him.
“Doctor,” the shaken Ryukhin asked in a whisper, “so he really is ill?”
“Oh, yes,” the doctor answered.
“But what is it he has?” Ryukhin asked timidly.
The weary doctor looked at Ryukhin and answered listlessly:
“Motor and speech agitation... delusional interpretations... a complicated case, apparently... Schizophrenia, one must suppose. And alcoholism on top of it...”
Ryukhin understood nothing of the doctor’s words except that things were evidently pretty bad for Ivan Nikolayevich. He sighed and asked:
“But why does he keep talking about some consultant?”
“He probably saw someone who struck his disordered imagination. Or perhaps he was hallucinating...”

A few minutes later the truck was carrying Ryukhin off to Moscow. Day was breaking, and the light of the streetlamps along the highway, not yet put out, was no longer needed and was unpleasant. The driver was angry at having lost the night, drove the truck as hard as he could, and it skidded on the bends.

And now the forest fell away, was left somewhere behind, and the river went off somewhere to one side; all manner of odds and ends came pouring toward the truck: fences with sentry boxes and stacks of firewood, very tall poles and some sort of masts, with spools strung on the masts, heaps of crushed stone, earth striped with channels—in a word, one felt that here it was, any minute now, Moscow, right there, just beyond the bend, about to tumble down on you and engulf you.

Ryukhin was shaken and tossed about; some stump of wood on which he had settled kept trying to slip out from under him. The restaurant towels, thrown in by the policeman and Panteley, who had left earlier by trolleybus, were sliding all over the platform. Ryukhin tried to gather them up, but, hissing for some reason with spite, “Oh, the devil take them! Why am I, really, fussing about like a fool?..”, he kicked them away and stopped looking at them.

The traveler’s state of mind was dreadful. It was becoming clear that his visit to the house of sorrow had left a very grievous mark on him. Ryukhin tried to understand what was tormenting him. The corridor with the blue lamps, stuck in his memory? The thought that there is no worse misfortune in the world than losing one’s reason? Yes, yes, of course, that too. But that—well, that was a general thought. There was something else. What was it? Hurt pride, that was it. Yes, yes, the hurtful words Bezdomny had flung right in his face. And the trouble was not that they were hurtful, but that there was truth in them.
The poet no longer looked about him, but, staring at the dirty, shaking floor, began to mutter something, to whine, gnawing at himself.

Yes, poems... He was thirty-two years old! Really, what next? And next he would go on composing a few poems a year. Until old age? Yes, until old age. And what would these poems bring him? Fame? “What rubbish! At least don’t fool yourself. Fame will never come to someone who writes bad poems. Why are they bad? He told the truth, the truth!” Ryukhin addressed himself mercilessly. “I don’t believe in anything I write!..”

Poisoned by this outburst of neurasthenia, the poet swayed, and the floor beneath him stopped shaking. Ryukhin raised his head and saw that he had long been in Moscow and, what was more, that dawn was over Moscow, that a cloud was lit up with gold, that his truck was standing, stuck in a column of other vehicles at the turn onto the boulevard, and that very close to him, on a pedestal, stood a metal man, his head slightly bowed, looking indifferently at the boulevard.

Some strange thoughts flooded into the ailing poet’s head. “There’s an example of real luck...” Here Ryukhin rose to his full height on the platform of the truck and raised his arm, for some reason attacking the cast-iron man, who was bothering no one. “Whatever step he took in life, whatever happened to him, it all went to his advantage, it all turned to his glory! But what did he do? I can’t comprehend it... Is there anything special in these words: ‘The storm with darkness veils...’? I don’t understand!.. Luck, luck!” Ryukhin suddenly concluded venomously, and felt the truck stir under him. “He shot, that White Guard shot at him, and shattered his hip, and secured him immortality...”

The column moved off. Completely ill, and even aged, the poet walked onto the veranda of Griboyedov’s no more than two minutes later. It was already deserted. In a corner some company was finishing its drinks, and in the middle of it a familiar master of ceremonies in a skullcap, with a glass of Abrau in his hand, was bustling about.

Ryukhin, burdened with towels, was greeted cordially by Archibald Archibaldovich and at once relieved of the cursed rags. Had Ryukhin not been so worn out in the clinic and on the truck, he would probably have taken pleasure in telling how everything had gone at the hospital and embellishing the story with invented details. But just now he was in no mood for it, and besides, unobservant as Ryukhin was, now, after the torture in the truck, for the first time he looked sharply at the pirate and understood that although he asked questions about Bezdomny and even exclaimed “Tut-tut-tut!”, in essence he was completely indifferent to Bezdomny’s fate and did not pity him in the least. “Good for him! Quite right!” Ryukhin thought with cynical, self-annihilating spite, and, breaking off his story about schizophrenia, he asked:
“Archibald Archibaldovich, I could do with a little vodka...”
The pirate put on a sympathetic face and whispered:
“I understand... this very minute...” And he waved to a waiter.

A quarter of an hour later Ryukhin, entirely alone, sat hunched over a smoked rybets, drinking glass after glass, understanding and admitting that nothing in his life could be put right any more, it could only be forgotten.

The poet had wasted his night while others feasted, and now understood that it could not be brought back. He had only to raise his head from the lamp to the sky to understand that the night was lost irretrievably. The waiters were hurriedly snatching the tablecloths off the tables. The cats prowling near the veranda had a morning look. Day was bearing down on the poet irresistibly.
